title: Microsoft brings AI inference closer to enterprise data with Windows Server 2028
summary: Microsoft is betting on a hybrid future where AI inferencing takes place where it makes the most sense. Which, logically, is where data already lives: On enterprise-controlled infrastructure. To that end, this week at Microsoft Ignite , the tech giant announced Windows Server 2028, its largest platform update since Windows Server 2025. Now in public preview, the next generation server is positioned as a foundation for AI inference that supports “enterprise hybrid intelligence.” It introduces new AI accelerators so enterprises can run inference on their own infrastructure, storage tools for accelerated data transfer, security controls to establish a “secure baseline from day one,” and simplified admin and management dashboards. But while it promises new capabilities across automation, management, identity, security, recovery, storage, and virtualization, it’s still early days for Windows Server 2028, with various features at different levels of availability and maturity. “It’s important to remember that this is the public preview phase, so a lot still remains a promise on the roadmap,” noted Infotech associate VP John Annand . Supporting enterprises where they are Windows Server 2028 gives customers the ability to run inferencing workloads close to physical operations and in their own controlled ecosystems. This means they don’t have to build and operate a “separate AI stack for every location,” Windows Server product team leader Neil Hinnant explained in a blog post . Microsoft is introducing AI accelerators in its servers; notably, AMD’s Instinct MI350P card is be in preview in the first half of 2027 for supported Windows Server systems, including Server 2028. The company is also developing tools to manage that hardware, deploy and configure inference environments , and direct model requests to appropriate environments. title: Ram through datacentres no one wants and hope the AI bubble never bursts: that’s the UK’s growth plan | George Monbiot
summary: The government doesn’t know what they are going to be used for, but that’s beside the point. Their real purpose is to sustain the share price of big tech It should have the status of an economic law: the sectors a government does most to promote in the name of growth are the sectors most likely to tank the economy. In the UK and the US, deregulation was meant to turn the financial sector into a never-ending growth machine. We have not yet fully recovered from the crash it helped cause in 2008. Fossil fuels are the most heavily subsidised sector on Earth. All that public money makes us highly vulnerable to oil price shocks, the whims of autocrats and societal collapse caused by climate breakdown. As for the great growth priority of our time – AI and datacentres – well, don’t take it from me. As Anthropic’s IPO prospectus warns , advanced AI systems could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity”. One thing we learned from the US midterm elections is that the drive to build datacentres is less a function of real commercial demand than of the need to sustain the share price of the big tech companies. After citizens across the US voted for moratoria on new datacentres, tech stocks , which have become dangerously dominant, plummeted, triggering fears of wider contagion . Whether new datacentres are required or not, we must keep building them, because confidence depends on them, and without that confidence the bubble will pop. The more you build, and the more this value dependency grows, the bigger the bubble becomes. George Monbiot is a Guardian columnist Continue reading...

title: At Apple, the robots are coming
summary: An Industrial Automation 2026 report claims US manufacturing has spent $51 billion on robotics and automation this year. It also says spending will exceed $84 billion by 2030. It claims industrial use of robotics is moving to full-scale deployment. I’m in no doubt that Apple is part of this. “Global industrial robot stock hit roughly 5.0 million units in 2025, up 9% year-over-year, and annual installations topped 600,000 units, up 11%, per the International Federation of Robotics. China installed 354,000 of them, 59% of the global total, up from 54% in 2024,” the report states. The Association for Advancing Automation (A3) shares its own recent data that shows US companies purchased almost 11,000 robots last year, up 24.8% from the prior 12 months. “What stands out in the third quarter is not simply the magnitude of the growth, but how broadly it was distributed across the market,” A3 executive vice president Alex Shikany said. What about Apple, then? Even since Apple introduced us to Daisy , its first product disassembly robot, we have known Apple dabbles in robotics . Most recently we learned that new Apple CEO John Ternus is bullish about robotics , and we now expect the first consumer robotics products to emerge from the company in 2027 or 2028 . Apple is not named specifically in the Industrial Automation report, but several of its active partners are mentioned. Schneider Electric and Cognex are both in the Apple supply chain. The first company now manufactures Apple Home Collection products to be sold at Apple retail stores from next month. The second is thought to make specialized machine vision systems used in Apple’s iPhone display production. title: Organizing Intelligence
summary: A powerful AI model does not automatically make a powerful organization. In Organizing Intelligence, Alex Imas, Andrew Koh and Shane Legg ask how human and artificial capabilities combine inside firms, and why coordination may matter as much as individual expertise. Their theoretical model separates improvements in task competence from improvements in working together. That distinction changes the possible paths of firm size, market concentration, wages and employment. Complementary human skills can sustain productive teams even when AI outperforms the average individual; stronger AI coordination can, under specified conditions, reorganize production around much larger firms. The paper also distinguishes gradual replacement within mixed teams from abrupt displacement when AI firms outcompete human firms. These are conditional economic mechanisms, illustrated by mathematical examples rather than forecasts of when jobs will disappear. The study offers a demanding question for AI evaluation: how should we measure the capabilities of an organization, rather than those of a model working alone?
author: The Bible of AI

title: How does a radar tell a hand gesture from everyday movement?
summary: Can a miniature radar recognise a hand command and leave the music playing when someone reaches for a cup? A millimetre-wave receiver follows distance and motion in darkness, giving an AI system a way to interpret a gesture without a camera. The difficulty is deciding where one command ends and whether a response is warranted at all. Experiments with continuous movements show how a slow swipe can produce two predictions. A separate phone study measured false activations per hour while people carried out ordinary tasks and while they deliberately repeated movements resembling swipes. Results from Europe and Asia show what changes with a new user, a different room or a second person nearby. Measurements on a working prototype also reveal how much of the power budget belongs to the radar itself. Together these studies suggest what to measure in a touch-free interface intended for everyday use.
author: The Bible of AI

title: When AI raises demand for chips, where does the value go?
summary: AI increases demand for the chips that make computing possible, but the value generated does not remain in one company or country. Design, fabrication, equipment and skilled work connect the European Union, the United States and major Asian production centres. This article follows those connections through revised market statistics, an executive survey and institutional research. Rising sales can support investment and innovation, while prices, production bottlenecks and market concentration complicate the distribution of gains. Public support also requires evidence that it produces benefits beyond activity that would have happened anyway. Separate regional indicators show why headquarters, factory capacity and value-chain revenue must not be confused. For workers and communities, the relevant outcomes include useful training, safe employment and durable local capabilities. The question is how expanding demand becomes productive investment whose benefits can be measured and shared.
author: The Bible of AI

title: When AI needs more power, who pays for the infrastructure?
summary: AI depends on physical infrastructure, and the costs of expanding it do not fall automatically on those who benefit. This article examines electricity demand, grid investment and the allocation of risk around data centres. It brings together separate European Union and United States estimates, Chinese demand evidence, and policy examples from Japan and Singapore. A global projection is presented alongside an operator survey, with their different purposes and limitations made explicit. More computing capacity may support innovation and useful services, but announced investment is not a measure of realised productivity. For households and smaller businesses, the relevant question is whether new demand pays for the capacity it requires. For workers and communities, it also concerns skills, reliable services and access to the benefits. The economic test begins with who bears the cost when a project grows, changes or fails to arrive.
author: The Bible of AI

title: When AI helps write software, what changes for workers?
summary: AI assistance can change how software is produced, but a completed task is only one part of dependable work. This article examines what happens to verification, professional judgement and opportunities to learn when generating a proposed solution becomes easier. It profiles related software service industries in the European Union and the United States, while keeping their statistical boundaries distinct. Company experiments and research on experienced open-source developers produce different results under different conditions. A 2026 professional survey adds a further perspective: trust often depends on being able to check the output. Read alongside the International Labour Organization's assessment, the evidence supports a careful distinction between changing tasks and changing employment. The central question is how organisations turn technical assistance into reliable services, sustainable workloads and meaningful opportunities for the people doing the work.

Time and again, a safety researcher or engineer walks out of the door with a public warning that commercial pressures are overriding safety guardrails. Last month, the person who oversaw safety reports for OpenAI’s product releases said he was quitting the ChatGPT creator because the company’s culture was “broken” and the entire AI industry was too careless in developing the technology. The previous month it was a researcher at OpenAI’s rival Anthropic who quit, warning that he believed AI “could kill us all by the end of the decade”. title: Six data protection myths cloud-native teams need to stop believing
summary: Cloud teams spend a lot of time and money designing applications to withstand failure. Replication, versioning, snapshots, and infrastructure as code (IaC) keep applications available and cloud environments more resilient. The trouble starts when teams assume those same capabilities will also allow them to recover from a cyberattack. In September 2026, Microsoft detailed an incident in which attackers used compromised Azure identities to delete cloud resources and target recovery protections. In a destructive sequence lasting about seven minutes, attackers attempted more than 100 deletions of storage accounts and deleted most of them. The attack shows how easily an attacker with sufficient privileges can turn cloud management capabilities against the organization. In talking with customers, I’ve learned they typically take one of two paths. Some spend heavily on disaster recovery because they’re worried about the next hyperscaler outage, while others assume that data sitting in AWS or Azure is already sufficiently protected. Both sides often misunderstand what cloud-native resilience tools were designed to do. Those tools behave differently when the disruption comes from an attacker instead of an outage. Here are six misconceptions I hear most. Myth 1: Amazon S3 versioning is the same as backup Versioning is useful when someone accidentally overwrites or deletes an object, but not when an attacker has your credentials. In January 2025, researchers at Halcyon documented the Codefinger ransomware campaign , in which attackers used compromised AWS credentials and Amazon S3’s server-side encryption with customer-provided keys (SSE-C) to make data inaccessible, then threatened deletion through S3 life-cycle policies. You should know who can change the controls protecting your data, particularly when the credentials used to access production can also alter life-cycle policies or other S3 settings. Neon can work across large code repositories, performing multi-file debugging and refactoring while making targeted changes to existing code, according to Google. Within Google’s Antigravity development environment, Neon can also orchestrate multiple Gemini 4 Hydrogen subagents working in parallel. Neon ranked first on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index with a score of 58.6, while achieving 65.2% on Terminal-Bench 4.1, a benchmark used to evaluate AI agents performing tasks in terminal environments, Google said. Google is positioning Neon between Gemini 4 Carbon, designed for demanding projects, and Gemini 4 Hydrogen, which prioritizes faster execution. The company has set Neon’s API pricing at $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens. Cached inputs cost $0.15 per million tokens, while the model supports a context window of up to one million tokens. Google said Neon delivered a 32% lower cost per task than Gemini 4 Carbon at the default high reasoning setting in Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index evaluations. It also reported savings of roughly 50% to 80% against leading competing models on the Vals Index and Agent Arena benchmarks. Neon offers four reasoning levels, allowing developers to adjust computational effort according to workload requirements. The model is being made available through the Gemini API in Google AI Studio and through Gemini for Business, with access also expanding to Google’s Antigravity development platform. title: PostgreSQL 19 Released
summary: PostgreSQL 19 Released Most years PostgreSQL ships a new release in September, but this year's release came two months later thanks mainly to the flurry of issues that the PostgreSQL team needed to address as part of the ongoing AI-reported vulnerability apocalypse. This release was definitely worth the wait. My favorite new feature is this one: For applications that send reads to standbys, PostgreSQL 19 adds "read-your-writes" consistency with the new WAIT FOR LSN command. A session on a standby can use WAIT FOR LSN to wait until the standby has replayed the write-ahead log (WAL) up to a specific log sequence number (LSN) before running a query, so the application can read data it just wrote on the primary. In practice, that looks like this: UPDATE movie SET genre = 'Dramatic' WHERE genre = 'Drama'; SELECT pg_current_wal_insert_lsn(); That returns a value like 0/0306EE20 . Store that somewhere (a signed cookie would work) such that on a subsequent request your application can do: WAIT FOR LSN '0/0306EE20' WITH (TIMEOUT '0.1s'); SELECT * FROM movie WHERE genre = 'Drama'; The timeout is optional - if you provide one you'll get an error if the replica you are talking to doesn't catch up within the specified time. I first encountered this pattern in Wikipedia , which has a hand-rolled version of this built against MySQL replication: In addition to this, MediaWiki attempts to ensure that the user sees events occurring on the wiki in chronological order. A few seconds of lag can be tolerated, as long as the user sees a consistent picture from subsequent requests. This is done by saving the primary binlog position in the session, and then at the start of each request, waiting for the replica to catch up to that position before doing any reads from it. Here's the relevant MediaWiki code , which these days uses MySQL's WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET() function and falls back to MASTER_POS_WAIT() .
